newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador voters support ouster of Bucaram -- polls.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador voters support ouster of Bucaram -- polls.

text.p: Ecuadoreans on Sunday endorsed in a plebiscite the February ouster of President Abdala Bucaram and the naming of Congress chairman Fabian Alarcon as interim president, according to an exit poll and projections.

One exit poll and a projection based on early returns by two separate firms showed 74 percent of Ecuadoreans endorsed the removal of Bucaram after Congress declared him "mentally insane" six months after taking office.

Three separate polling companies also showed that between 62 and 65 percent of voters endorsed Alarcon as interim president. Alarcon will rule until August 1998, when he will be replaced by a new president to be elected in May next year.
Immediately after the preliminary results were released, Alarcon said he planned to reshuffle his Cabinet.
"The people showed today that they want to participate in Ecuador's political process. I think we need some adjustments and restructuring at a national level," Alarcon said.

Alarcon, leader of the small Alfarista Radical Front that opposes Bucaram's Roldosista Party, asked Ecuador's 6.9-million-strong electorate to vote in a plebiscite in response to criticism of his government's legitimacy.
The plebiscite's official results are expected early next month.

Bucaram, a populist leader who boasted during the presidential race that "I do whatever the hell I like," campaigned by jumping from a helicopter in a Batman outfit. After taking office he recorded and performed his rock album "A Madman in Love," accompanied by young female singers.
The government deployed 64,000 soldiers and policemen to guard the country's 23,000 polling stations on Sunday. No incidents were reported.

Bucaram, who is wanted in Ecuador on charges of mishandling public funds, profiteering and corruption, has denounced Alarcon from Panama, where he sought political asylum two days after being removed from power.
The ousted leader accuses Alarcon of orchestrating his ouster with the military. Both the interim president and the armed forces deny the charges.
